newsitem.title: CANADA: Canadian equities may suffer setback in spring.
newsitem.headline: Canadian equities may suffer setback in spring.

text.p: The winter's bull run in Canadian equities may lumber on for a few more weeks, but the Ides of March is likely to prove a dangerous time for the market and could spark a sharp correction.

Analysts said March 1, the end of the registered retirement savings plan (RRSP) season in which Canadians are allowed to plunge money into tax sheltered investments for the current tax year, will stem the flood of cash from swollen funds into the market.
By mid-March, most fund managers will have finished deciding where to put even late arriving money.

Market strategists agree that the reduced liquidity will make the market more volatile while some bears think stock investors should heed the adage Julius Caesar ignored: beware the middle -- as well as the end -- of March.

The Toronto Stock Exchange key index of 300 stocks was up 5.63 percent when it hit an all-time high of 6260.73 on Wednesday, said Craig Hurl, the TSE coordinator of special index projects. It was trading at 6209.60, up 4.53 points, late morning on Friday.
Any correction coming from the United States would accentuate a downtrend in Canadian equities, analysts said.

"I have a feeling we are about to see a correction in the American market, a rather significant one. I think it will be accompanied by a correction in the Canadian market," said Michael Metz, chief investment strategist at Oppenheimer & Co.
"I think it's underway. I think it's begun and I think the retreat in the bond market has begun as well...I think it's beginning this week and will gain momentum on the downside next week," he added.
U.S. Federal Reserve chairman Alan Greenspan addresses Congress with his closely watched semi-annual Humphrey-Hawkins testimony on Tuesday and Wednesday next week.

"He's going to say clearly the risks of inflation moving higher are greater than the risks of the economy slipping into recession. I certainly wouldn't rule out an interest rate rise as early as March 25," said Stephen Lewis, director of research at London Bond Broking.

Chase Manhattan Bank said on Thursday its global asset management operations are underweight on high-priced U.S. and Canadian equities as well as the U.K. and Japan and overweight in continental Europe, Latin America and South-East Asia.
Analysts are still uncertain about the possible magnitude of a pull-back.
Montreal-based strategist Bill Ram said the Canadian market could correct five to eight percent once it peaks.
HSBC James Capel analyst Bob Boaz has a target for the TSE 300 this year of 6600. He said it would be quite possible to see a 10 percent correction from that level.
"I think you have got at least 10 percent on the market. It's quite possible to see something like a 5300 to 5500 TSE on the correction in the spring," he said.
However, technical analyst Ron Meisels, president of Montreal-based P and C Holdings, saw strong support at 6100 -- just 160 points below current levels.

A rotation into battered sub-sectors like gold and energy could cushion the fall somewhat, said CIBC Wood Gundy market strategist Subodh Kumar. "It will be more volatile...It's difficult to say (whether the market will fall after RRSP season ends) but from the fundamental point of view, I think it's going to take a Fed hike for us to have a correction."
A mitigating force in early March will be the flow of capital from fund managers investing for latecomers.
Mutual fund investors often wait until the eleventh hour of the deadline day to make decisions. And brokerages and mutual funds will man their desks past midnight on March 1.
It could take up to four weeks for the last trickles of cash to run out as funds need to weigh their decisions carefully, analysts said.
But the period from mid-March until May could be stormy for the market -- particularly if a U.S. market correction materializes, Boaz said.
"I think probably a high-risk period is going to be April and May," he added.
